sections.title: Intermediate Concept of Number Series
sections.content: At Level 2, single-step logic is no longer enough. The series will feature rapid growth (multiplication), dual patterns (alternate series), or require you to find the 'difference of differences' (Double Difference).

sections.title: Double Difference Method
sections.content: When the first layer of differences does not reveal a clear pattern, find the difference of those differences. This second layer often forms a simple arithmetic progression or constant.

sections.title: Mixed Operations (Multiply + Add/Subtract)
sections.content: The most frequently tested banking and SSC pattern. The series grows quickly but not by exact multiples. The pattern takes the form of (x1 + 1), (x2 + 2), (x3 + 3) or (x2 - 1), (x2 - 2), etc.

sections.title: Alternate (Twin) Series
sections.content: Two different series are merged into one. The pattern jumps over one number. If a series fluctuates (increases, then decreases, then increases), it is almost always an alternate series.

sections.title: Decimal Multiplication (0.5 Pattern)
sections.content: If a series decreases suddenly at the second term, and then starts increasing (e.g., 10, 5, 6, 10.5), it involves multiplication by decimals like 0.5, 1.5, 2.5.

sections.title: Square & Cube Offsets (n² ± x)
sections.content: Numbers are generated by adding or subtracting the base number itself to its square or cube. Examples: n² + n (2, 6, 12, 20) or n³ - n (0, 6, 24, 60).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Giving up when the first difference fails (not checking double difference). 2. Not noticing the 'dip and rise' which signals the 0.5 multiplication rule. 3. Confusing alternate series with random numbers.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 2 requires evaluating the speed of growth. Sharp growth = Multiplication/Squares. Fluctuation = Alternate Series. Initial dip followed by growth = 0.5 Decimal Multiplication. Constant slow growth without clear first gaps = Double Difference.

tricks.title: The Growth Rate Check
tricks.explanation: Look at the last two terms. If the last term is more than double the previous term, the series is definitely based on multiplication. If not, use the difference method.

tricks.title: The 'Dip and Rise' 0.5 Trick
tricks.explanation: If the second number is exactly or nearly half of the first number, start by multiplying by 0.5.

tricks.title: Double Difference Default
tricks.explanation: If a series is gently increasing (no multiplication) and layer 1 makes no sense, immediately write layer 2 without thinking.
tricks.example: Series: 5, 12, 24, 43, 71. Gaps: 7, 12, 19, 28. Gaps of Gaps: 5, 7, 9. Next gap of gap = 11. Next gap = 28+11 = 39. Next term = 71+39 = 110.

tricks.title: The Zig-Zag (Alternate) Identifier
tricks.explanation: If the numbers go UP, DOWN, UP, DOWN, split the series into odd-positioned terms and even-positioned terms.

tricks.title: n² ± n vs n² ± 1
tricks.explanation: Memorize the sequence 2, 6, 12, 20, 30. This is always 1²+1, 2²+2, 3²+3. It saves massive calculation time.
tricks.example: If you see 12, 20, 30, 42... the next is 7²+7 = 56.
